question: Did Jesus claim to be God?
subtitle: Is the Trinity original Christianity?
aliases: is the Trinity in the Bible
did Jesus say he was God
the Father is greater than I
I and the Father are one
finding: Be precise about the target, because the easy version attacks a doctrine nobody holds. We are not arguing the New Testament fails to distinguish Father from Son; Trinitarianism asserts that too. The claim is narrower: nothing Jesus says asserts what Nicaea asserts, one identical substance and co-equality. In the red text the traffic runs one way: the Father is greater, the Father is the only true God, authority is given to the Son, the Son does not know the day. The doctrine that resolves those texts is a fourth- and fifth-century product with a datable construction history. And what Jesus actually taught was participatory divinity: the unity he had with the Father is the unity he prays his followers will have. This is not an attack on reverence for Jesus. It's the difference between worshipping a ceiling and being shown a floor.
oneLiners: We're not arguing Jesus isn't distinct from the Father; your own doctrine says that. We're asking where he ever says he's the same substance.
"The Father is greater than I." That's not our reading. That's the quote.
Authority given. A day he doesn't know. A God he calls "my God." The traffic in those verses only runs one direction.
The one verse that states the Trinity outright isn't in a single Greek manuscript until the 14th century, and no Greek father ever quotes it.
Jesus got accused of claiming to be God, and his defense was "Scripture says you all are."
doNotSay: "Jesus is distinct from the Father, so the Trinity is false." Pointing at two speakers in one sentence refutes modalism, not Nicaea.
Don't dismiss John when it's inconvenient. We quote John constantly on this card; every argument has to work inside John, and it does.
Don't date the Comma Johanneum to the 16th century. No Greek manuscript before the 14th; being corrected on this is expensive.
Don't deploy "be perfect" as "a command, not a compliment." Teleios is completeness; the context is enemy-love. See what-we-actually-offer.
Don't say Nicaea forged Matthew 28:19. Every Greek manuscript has the formula and Irenaeus quotes it around 180. The defensible point: Matthew wrote it, and nobody in Acts baptizes with it.

sources.note: Jesus declines the adjective on the grounds that it belongs to God alone. Matthew and Luke both soften it, which is the expected direction of change.
In Jesus's own prayer, in the latest and most exalted gospel: the Father is "the only true God" and Jesus is the one sent. Preserved by a high-Christology author against his own program.

sources.phrase: my Father is greater than I
sources.note: The standard reply is economic subordination, role not substance. Coherent on its own terms, and a fourth-century framework applied backwards to texts that never supply the correction themselves.

sources.phrase: The Son can do nothing of himself
sources.note: John 5:18 is the narrator reporting what opponents concluded ("making himself equal with God"); verse 19 is Jesus's reply, the flattest subordination statement in the gospel.

sources.phrase: All power is given unto me
sources.note: Authority is given. The same "given" as Daniel 7:14, and the same delegated vocabulary as Mark 2:10. A God who lacked authority is the problem Chalcedon has to solve.

sources.phrase: to my God, and your God
sources.note: Eleven verses before Thomas's confession, Jesus calls the Father his God. Within John, theos applied to Jesus cannot mean something John has already had Jesus deny.

sources.phrase: neither the Son, but the Father
sources.note: He admits he does not know something. Ehrman (The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture) documents later scribes deleting "nor the Son" from the parallel at Matthew 24:36: the change moves toward the copyist's theology and away from his source.

The sentence after "I and the Father are one," when they pick up stones. His defense is not "I alone am God" but "Scripture calls all of you gods." Jesus has authorized a non-homoousios sense in which a human can be called god. Keep it in hand for John 20:28.
If John 10:30 proves unique deity, John 17:22 grants it to everyone and 14:12 has them surpassing him. Ours is a higher anthropology, not a lower Christology.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 108, 13, 3
sources.note: "He who will drink from my mouth will become like me." The goal is becoming, not worshipping; what Eastern Orthodoxy carried forward as theosis. Demote from proof to parallel: lead with the red text and let Thomas confirm.

sources.tier: red text · John · the strongest verse for the other side
sources.note: Thomas says it and Jesus does not correct him. Raise it before they do. Jesus's reply is a rebuke about seeing and believing (20:29); the evangelist's own summary of the confession is a messianic title (20:31); Jesus called the Father "my God" eleven verses earlier (20:17); and the usage has Hebrew precedent (Psalm 45:6, Exodus 7:1, Psalm 82:6).

sources.tier: red text · the strongest Synoptic text, and our criterion cuts against us
sources.phrase: sitting on the right hand of power
sources.note: Asked if he is the Messiah, Mark's Jesus says "I am" and adds Daniel 7. Matthew and Luke hedge it, so Mark's is the harder reading and probably earlier. We won't argue it away. Daniel 7's figure comes to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion: two beings and a transfer. Enthronement is enormous, and it is not consubstantiality.

sources.phrase: power on earth to forgive sins
sources.note: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" His answer is not "because I am God" but that the Son of Man has authority (exousia) on earth to forgive sins, and he hands that authority on (John 20:23, Matthew 18:18). A power given and then given away is not evidence of unique divine substance.

The Exodus 3:14 echo is real and we concede it. Three limits: the healed blind man says "I am" one chapter later (9:9); pre-existence is a different claim than co-equal substance (Wisdom, Torah, the Messiah's name in 1 Enoch 48:3 all pre-exist); and it is John alone, six chapters before "the Father is greater than I."

sources.phrase: I myself also am a man
sources.note: "He accepts worship (proskuneō)." The verb means prostration before a superior and is used of people. The tell is what happens where exclusive divine worship is meant: Peter pulls Cornelius off the floor, Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes (Acts 14), the angel in Revelation refuses it twice. Those writers knew the difference and marked it.

sources.tier: early church · our own star witness
sources.title: Didache 7, the triune baptismal formula
sources.note: "Your early Didache baptizes in the triune name." Triadic naming is not homoousios, and that distinction is the entire card. Matthew 28:19, 2 Corinthians 13:14 and 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 name three too, and we list them. The Didache's own Christology calls Jesus God's pais, servant or child; its prayers have no incarnation. Don't lead with a date adjustment; argument one is sufficient.

sources.phrase: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost
sources.note: Names three. Does not assert one substance in three co-equal persons, which is the claim at issue. Same answer as the Didache.

sources.tier: KJV prints it · no Greek manuscript before the 14th century
sources.note: The Comma Johanneum. The KJV has it; the Greek tradition doesn't until Codex Ottobonianus (GA 629), and no Greek father cites it once through the whole Arian controversy. Newton's argument holds: if that verse had existed in 325, Nicaea would have quoted it constantly, and nobody did.

sources.title: Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon; Tertullian coins trinitas c. 213
sources.edition: NPNF series 2 vol. 14 (the councils), public domain; Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988), in copyright
sources.note: Three-fold naming is first-generation; co-equal substance is not. The men who first theorized the triad ranked it (Justin, Tertullian, Origen). Nicaea's creed says of the Spirit only "and in the Holy Spirit"; co-equality for the Spirit arrives in 381; the ousia/hypostasis vocabulary isn't stable until the end of the century; the two-natures formula most apologetic answers depend on is 451. Position claims by paraphrase: no primary texts for these fathers held here.
